captions.text: Project time.
We're building an AI resume analyzer: give it a resume and a job posting, and it
writes a skills-gap report.
It uses everything from this module: versioned prompts, structured outputs, task
decomposition, grounding checks, and evaluations.
The input is a resume and a job posting, as plain text or Markdown files.
The output is a skills-gap report, in Markdown for people, or JSON for other
programs.
Every report records which prompt versions produced it, and what it cost.
And like Module 2, it runs offline with a fake API, it's fully tested, and it has an
evaluation set.
Here's the plan.
The command line calls the analyzer, which runs the pipeline: extract with the
model, compare in code, advise with the model.
It takes its prompts from the versioned registry, and its schemas from the Pydantic
models.
Skills handles different spellings and the grounding check, report formats the
result, and evals runs the analyzer on labelled cases.
And the client is either the real API, or the offline fake.
A word about the offline fake, because this project's output looks much more real
than Module 2's placeholders.
The fake speaks the Messages API protocol, so the real SDK runs unchanged.
But instead of a model, it uses keyword rules: it finds skill names from a fixed
list, and fills in the requested schema.
It's not a model.
It ignores the prompt wording, it misses negation, and it only knows a fixed list of
skills.
Every result you see in this video comes from these rules, because no API key was
used to record it.
A call records one model request: the prompt's label and fingerprint, the tokens,
and the cost.
A gap report holds the extracted profile and job, the comparison results, any skills
the grounding check dropped, the suggestions, and the calls.
The score and the experience gap are arithmetic, so they're properties computed in
code.
We never ask the model to do sums.
Resumes and job postings spell skills differently: Postgres or PostgreSQL, k8s or
Kubernetes.
The aliases table maps each spelling to one name.
Normalize collapses spaces, lowercases, and applies the aliases.
Now Postgres and PostgreSQL compare as equal.
Compare normalises the candidate's skills into a set.
Then each must-have is matched or missing, and each nice-to-have that's missing is
listed.
The results keep the job posting's own wording, so the report reads naturally.
Extract profile calls the structured method with the profile schema and low effort,
because extraction is simple.
Then the grounding check keeps only skills the resume really names.
Extract job does the same for the posting.
Suggest fills the advice template with the comparison results, and uses medium
effort, because writing good advice takes more judgment.
And analyze runs the pipeline.
Note the condition: if nothing is missing, code skips the advice call entirely.
That's one less model call, for free.
Let's run it on Sam, a fictional backend developer, and a fictional backend job
posting.
Five of six must-have skills: eighty-three percent.
Postgres in the resume matched PostgreSQL in the posting, thanks to normalisation,
and GitHub Actions counted as CI slash CD.
Kubernetes is missing.
And the footer records the three prompt versions with their fingerprints, the model,
the tokens, and the cost.
Offline, the tokens are estimates.
The model extracts, and code compares, scores, and decides.
Aliases make different spellings match.
And every report records its prompts, tokens, and cost.
In part two: the suggestions and the report, the command line, the full demo with
failures, the tests, and the evaluation.
Then we wrap up the module.
